why:
Best first platform, for four reasons.
• Work is mandated and recurring under 49 CFR 192: annual leak surveys in business districts, annual cathodic protection checks, rectifier checks six times a year and annual regulator-station inspections.
• Replacement is funded through state rate trackers, with bare steel running to ~2041 at UGI.
• The target universe is bounded and knowable: ~240 DCA members.
• It is the only unit with a real labor and fleet link to another unit. With water it shares ~53% of movable headcount and ~65% of fleet value (est.). It also ties into Imperial (meter brass, service and cable scrap), Transend (pipe freight) and Panther (fittings).

Risks:
• Artera, the largest gas roll-up, is highly leveraged (rated CCC+ in 2022).
• Centuri earns only 8.3%.
• Cast iron is finite (~16K miles left).
• The PHMSA leak rule was withdrawn.
• Compliance contracts are often re-bid on unit price.
tam: $12-20B/yr outsourced (est.), from AGA's $33-37B/yr safety spend; gas utility construction capex $49.1B (2023)
mro_share: High: safety and replacement programs ($33-37B/yr) are the bulk of the $49.1B of construction capex (rough, mixed AGA measures)

fragmentation: Moderate: ~240 DCA members; ~6 scaled players (Centuri, Artera, Quanta, Michels, Primoris, MasTec)
competition: Public: Quanta (InfraSource, Hallen), Primoris (Snelson, ARB), MasTec, Centuri. Sponsor-backed: CD&R (Artera), Ridgemont (Sparus), MPE (Precision Pipeline, Delphi), MidOcean, Graycliff, USIC; several hydrovac roll-ups.

Kiely is family-led (control unconfirmed). Sponsor-owned: Sparus (Ridgemont), Artera (CD&R). Danella has a safety flag.

why:
Best as the second unit, bolted onto the gas platform in the same metros, not as the first.

Strengths:
• It is the most fragmented unit, with one >$1B player (Azuria/Inframark).
• It has the second-largest candidate list, clustered in tank asset management and sewer cleaning.
• Tank asset-management contracts (multi-year, fixed annual fee) are the closest match in this report to recurring maintenance with switching costs.

Weaknesses:
• Most customers are municipalities buying by low bid.
• Lead-line replacement (LCRI, due Nov 2027) is in litigation.
• FY2026 was the last year of IIJA supplemental SRF money.
• Utilities do most O&M in-house.

why:
Largest and best-funded pool. EEI members spent ~$208B of capex in 2025 and plan >$1.1T for 2025-29. Aging is real (50-55% of distribution transformers are older than 33 years), and pole inspection and vegetation work recur on fixed cycles.

But it is the most picked-over unit:
• The only independent platform-grade candidate, Tomberlin Pole Treatment, is add-on scale.
• Sponsors have paid up: Pike (>$5B reported), United Utility Services (~$1B), East Coast Power.
• Public peers trade at ~15.2x.
• Lineworkers need ~3.5-year apprenticeships, and IBEW jurisdiction keeps crews separate.
• Vegetation work is thin-margin and storm work is episodic.

Run T&D as a separate operating company later, entering through a lower-middle-market distribution-maintenance or substation-testing firm.

why:
Smallest pool, and partly shrinking:
• Coal units average 45 years and retire at ~50.
• OEM long-term service agreements and in-house staff take much of the ~$13B of maintenance spend.
• Outage work is lumpy and seasonal.

Nuclear life extension (80-year licenses) is a real tailwind, but Appendix B quality requirements and Day & Zimmermann's multi-year fleet contracts protect incumbents. The precedents are the weakest of the four units: Williams went through Chapter 11, and Team earned 2.7-6.8%.

Enter only through NETA testing or NDE add-ons, which are already being rolled up (Shermco, RESA).
